name: Sciatica / Lumbosacral Radicular Pain
status: Gold chapter draft - source checked, clinician validation pending
definition: A clinical syndrome of radiating lower-limb pain caused by irritation or pathology of one or more lumbosacral nerve roots. True radicular pain should be distinguished from non-radicular referred leg pain, hip/SI disorders, peripheral neuropathy and vascular causes.
anatomy: Lumbar and sacral nerve roots contributing to the lumbosacral plexus and sciatic nerve pathway.
Common symptomatic levels are L4-L5 and L5-S1, but clinical localization must be based on the full neurological pattern rather than MRI alone.
etiology: Lumbar disc herniation/protrusion/extrusion with nerve-root irritation or compression.
Foraminal or lateral recess stenosis; degenerative canal stenosis.
Degenerative spondylolisthesis or other structural narrowing.
Less common serious causes: infection, malignancy, fracture/trauma, inflammatory disease or other space-occupying pathology.
riskFactors: Recurrent/heavy spinal loading or occupational exposure may contribute in some patients.
Smoking, obesity, deconditioning and psychosocial factors may influence back-pain burden and recovery, but should not be used alone to deny appropriate specialist referral.
presentation: Low-back or buttock pain radiating into the leg, often below the knee.
Shooting, electric, burning or sharp leg pain.
Possible focal weakness, reflex change or gait difficulty.
Symptoms may worsen with cough, sneeze, strain or certain spinal positions; pattern is variable.
redFlags: NEW bladder dysfunction: retention, difficulty initiating/maintaining stream, loss of bladder sensation or new incontinence.
NEW bowel dysfunction or loss of bowel sensation/control.
NEW saddle/perineal/genital sensory change or altered sensation when wiping.
Rapidly progressive or severe motor weakness, new foot drop, or major gait deterioration.
Severe bilateral radicular symptoms, especially with sphincter/saddle symptoms.
Fever/systemic illness, immunosuppression, IV drug use or concern for spinal infection.
Known cancer, unexplained weight loss, destructive bone pain or suspected malignancy.
Significant trauma, osteoporosis, chronic steroid exposure or suspected fracture.
history: Exact pain map: back -> buttock -> thigh -> leg -> foot; side and dermatomal tendency.
Onset, mechanism, duration, progression, recurrence and night/rest pain.
Pain severity plus functional impact: sitting, standing, walking, sleep, work and ADL.
Numbness, tingling, weakness, falls, gait change, foot slap/foot drop.
Mandatory bladder, bowel, saddle/perineal and sexual-function screen when clinically relevant.
Fever, recent infection, TB exposure, cancer history, weight loss, immune suppression, steroid use, trauma.
Previous MRI/X-ray, injections, surgery, medications and response.
Workload, lifting, driving, posture, exercise, sleep, mood, fear avoidance and social/occupational barriers.
exam: Vitals and general screen when systemic/serious pathology is possible.
Gait: antalgic pattern; heel and toe walking when safe.
Lumbar posture and active range of motion.
Straight-leg raise (SLR) and crossed SLR; Slump may supplement but should not be used in isolation.
Motor testing: hip/knee/ankle/great-toe movements with side-to-side comparison.
Dermatomal light-touch/pinprick sensory examination as appropriate.
Knee (patellar) and ankle (Achilles) reflexes; compare sides.
Hip and sacroiliac screening when symptoms are atypical; peripheral pulses/vascular screen when claudication is possible.
Document objective neurological deficit clearly and repeat at follow-up if present.

rootMap.motor: great-toe extension, ankle dorsiflexion, hip abduction
rootMap.reflex: no single consistently reliable deep-tendon reflex

rootMap.typicalSensory: posterolateral calf/lateral or plantar foot tendency

differentials: Central canal stenosis with neurogenic claudication
Hip osteoarthritis or other hip pathology
Meralgia paraesthetica or other peripheral nerve syndromes
investigations: Do not routinely image uncomplicated low-back pain/sciatica in a non-specialist setting when serious pathology is not suspected.
Use MRI when serious pathology is suspected, when neurological deficit is progressive/significant, or in specialist/intervention planning when imaging is likely to change management.

For persistent/progressive symptoms after a suitable course of conservative management in a surgery/intervention candidate, lumbar MRI without contrast is generally the preferred initial advanced imaging.
Contrast-enhanced MRI may be appropriate in selected contexts such as suspected infection/malignancy or certain postoperative questions.
Radiographs/CT are selected for trauma, fracture risk, bony detail, alignment or other specific indications rather than routine radicular pain.
Laboratory tests are not routine for uncomplicated sciatica; order targeted CBC, ESR/CRP and disease-specific testing when infection, inflammatory disease or malignancy is suspected.
imagingCorrelation: Always match side, level and morphology to symptoms and neurological findings.
Degenerative disc bulges and other abnormalities may be incidental; an MRI report is not itself the diagnosis.
Document nerve-root compromise: central/paracentral/foraminal/extraforaminal location, lateral recess/foraminal stenosis, migration/sequestration and associated canal compromise when relevant.
management: Education and reassurance with individualized safety-net advice.
Encourage continuation/graded return to normal activity within tolerance; avoid prolonged bed rest.
Exercise/rehabilitation individualized to irritability, neurological status, function, preferences and comorbidity.
Manual therapy, if used, should be part of an exercise-based package rather than a stand-alone treatment.
Address sleep, fear avoidance, work barriers and psychosocial obstacles when they are materially affecting recovery.
Medication decisions require individualized contraindication/risk review; use the lowest effective dose for the shortest appropriate period when an NSAID is chosen.

Do not treat chronic sciatica with long-term opioids; NICE advises against gabapentinoids/other antiepileptics, oral corticosteroids and benzodiazepines for sciatica because overall benefit is lacking and harms exist.
Consider epidural local anaesthetic + steroid only in selected acute severe sciatica within an appropriate specialist pathway.
Urgent spinal assessment for cauda equina features or rapidly progressive major neurological deficit.
Consider surgical/decompression opinion when non-surgical care has not improved pain/function and imaging is concordant with the sciatic symptoms.
rehab: Acute/high-irritability: education, positions/movements that reduce symptoms, gentle mobility and frequent tolerable activity.
Recovery: progressive walking/aerobic activity, trunk/hip strength, mobility and movement-control exercises according to clinical response.
Return-to-work/activity: graded exposure to lifting, sitting, driving and occupational tasks; emphasize capacity and confidence.
Stop/reassess if neurological deficit is worsening, new red flags appear, or exercise produces persistent significant neurological deterioration.
outcomes: Patient-specific functional scale or activity goals

ayurvedaFramework.principle: Use as a parallel Ayurvedic diagnostic/documentation framework; do not assume one-to-one equivalence with every modern cause of radicular leg pain.
assessment: Dosha and Doshabheda including relevant Vata subtypes
ayurvedaFramework.clinicalFeatures: Classical symptom documentation may include Ruk, Toda, Stambha, Spandana and lower-limb radiating symptoms, with individualized examination.
ayurvedaFramework.treatmentSafety: Nidana Parivarjana, Shamana/Shodhana and Panchakarma choices must be individualized by bala, avastha, ama, comorbidities, structural pathology and contraindications. Red-flag spinal disease takes priority for urgent modern diagnostic/referral pathways.

patientHandout: Sciatica means pain traveling from the lower back/buttock into the leg because a lower-spine nerve root is irritated.
Keep moving within your tolerance. Long periods of complete bed rest usually do not help recovery.
Use your prescribed exercise/activity plan and build activity gradually.
Seek emergency care immediately for new bladder/bowel difficulty, numbness around the genitals/bottom, rapidly increasing leg weakness or severe symptoms in both legs.
An MRI is not required for every episode. It is most useful when serious disease is suspected or when the result will change specialist treatment.
researchNote: Recovered founder thesis observation (n=60): Vataja cases were interpreted as relatively degeneration-dominant, while Vata-Kaphaja cases showed a more obstructive/mass-effect pattern. This is a local observational finding and must not be treated as a universal diagnostic rule.
